claims.claim: Doctors' survival estimates at hospice referral were accurate in 1 in 5 and mostly too optimistic.
claims.supporting_passage: Median survival was 24 days. Only 20% (92/468) of predictions were accurate (within 33% of actual survival); 63% (295/468) were overoptimistic and 17% (81/468) were overpessimistic. Overall, doctors overestimated survival by a factor of 5.3.
claims.pico_timeframe: 468 terminally ill patients at hospice referral, Chicago, late 1990s; doctors' estimate vs actual survival
claims.safe_wording: In a US study of 468 people referred to hospice, doctors' estimates were within a third of actual survival about 20 in 100 times; 63 in 100 were too optimistic and 17 in 100 too pessimistic.
claims.qualifications: Define 'accurate' as within 33% of actual survival; US, one city, around 2000, mostly outpatient hospice referrals.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Old single study; newer review (White 2016) agrees estimates are often inaccurate.

claims.claim: Longer doctor-patient relationship was linked with less accurate prediction.
claims.supporting_passage: As duration of doctor-patient relationship increased and time since last contact decreased, prognostic accuracy decreased.
claims.safe_wording: In this one study, the longer the doctor had known the patient, and the more recently they had seen them, the less accurate the estimate tended to be.
claims.qualifications: Association in one study; does not prove that knowing the patient causes the error.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Not confirmed by a later review as far as checked.

claims.claim: A systematic review found clinicians' survival predictions in palliative care are frequently inaccurate, with no expert group.
claims.supporting_passage: Studies of prognostic accuracy in palliative care are heterogeneous, but the evidence suggests that clinicians' predictions are frequently inaccurate. No sub-group of clinicians was consistently shown to be more accurate than any other.
claims.pico_timeframe: 42 studies, adult palliative care; up to June 2015
claims.safe_wording: A review of 42 studies found clinicians' survival predictions in palliative care were often inaccurate, and no professional group was consistently better.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Probabilistic estimates tended to be more accurate (c 0.74-0.78).

claims.claim: Give a range, name what would shorten it, seek a colleague's view.

claims.supporting_passage: For the outcome of death at 6 to 18 months, the pooled prognostic characteristics were sensitivity 67.0% (95% confidence interval [CI] 55.7%-76.7%), specificity 80.2% (73.3%-85.6%), ... positive predictive value 37.1% (95% CI 30.2%-44.6%) and negative predictive value 93.1% (95% CI 91.0%-94.8%).
claims.safe_wording: Pooled across 16 studies, the question picked up about 67 in 100 people who died within 6 to 18 months; of those flagged, about 37 in 100 died in that window, so most flagged people were still alive.
claims.qualifications: PPV depends on how many in the group die, so varies by setting; window 6-18 months, not strictly a year.

claims.claim: Worse in non-cancer illness; most studies at moderate-high risk of bias.
claims.supporting_passage: The surprise question had worse discrimination in patients with noncancer illness (area under sROC curve 0.77 [95% CI 0.73-0.81]) than in patients with cancer (area under sROC curve 0.83 ... ). Most studies had a moderate to high risk of bias
claims.safe_wording: It worked less well in illnesses other than cancer, and most studies had a moderate to high risk of bias.

claims.claim: Surprise question is in Gold Standards Framework Proactive Identification Guidance.
claims.safe_wording: Omit, or say 'widely used in UK identification tools' only if another batch verifies it.

claims.claim: Use it as a prompt for conversation rather than prediction.
claims.supporting_passage: The surprise question performs poorly to modestly as a predictive tool for death
claims.safe_wording: The authors judged it a poor to modest predictor; using it to open conversations is our judgement.

claims.claim: Course of advanced dementia over 18 months.
claims.supporting_passage: Over a period of 18 months, 54.8% of the residents died. The probability of pneumonia was 41.1%; a febrile episode, 52.6%; and an eating problem, 85.8%.
claims.pico_timeframe: 323 US nursing-home residents with advanced dementia, 18 months
claims.safe_wording: In a US study of 323 care-home residents with advanced dementia, over 18 months about 86 in 100 developed eating problems, about 53 in 100 a fever, about 41 in 100 pneumonia, and about 55 in 100 died.
claims.qualifications: US nursing homes, advanced (late-stage) dementia; probabilities over 18 months.

claims.claim: Burdensome interventions in last 3 months and link with proxy understanding.
claims.supporting_passage: In the last 3 months of life, 40.7% of residents underwent at least one burdensome intervention (hospitalization, emergency room visit, parenteral therapy, or tube feeding). Residents whose proxies had an understanding of the poor prognosis and clinical complications expected in advanced dementia were much less likely to have burdensome interventions in the last 3 months of life than were residents whose proxies did not have this understanding (adjusted odds ratio, 0.12; 95% confidence interval, 0.04 to 0.37).
claims.pico_timeframe: Residents who died; proxy understanding vs not; last 3 months
claims.safe_wording: About 41 in 100 who died had a hospital transfer, emergency visit, drip or tube feeding in their last 3 months. Those whose families understood the likely course were much less likely to have these.
claims.qualifications: Observational; do not convert OR 0.12; does not prove that informing families causes the difference.

numbers.meaning: of decedents, >=1 burdensome intervention, last 3 months
adjusted, observational; state in words only

claims.claim: Functional decline patterns differ by trajectory; frail decedents low function throughout last year and more dependent near death.
claims.supporting_passage: cancer decedents were highly functional early in their final year but markedly more disabled 3 months prior to death ...; organ failure decedents experienced a fluctuating pattern of decline ...; and frail decedents were relatively more disabled in the final year and especially dependent during the last month (2.92 [2.24-3.60] vs 5.84 [5.33-6.35], P<.001). ... Trajectories of functional decline at the end of life are quite variable.
claims.pico_timeframe: 4190 US decedents aged 65+; ADL dependency in last year
claims.safe_wording: A large US study of older people found that those who died with frailty already needed help with daily activities a year before death and needed more near the end, while people dying of cancer often stayed independent until the last few months.
claims.qualifications: Group averages from 1980s-90s US data; individuals vary widely; dementia grouped under frailty in this study only by inference - do not claim dementia specifically from Lunney.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Murray 2005 (PMID 15860828, no abstract, not opened) describes three trajectories conceptually.

numbers.meaning: mean ADL dependencies, frail, 12 months vs last month

claims.claim: No clear moment; start conversations early.
claims.safe_wording: Present as judgement drawn from the slow-decline pattern.

claims.claim: Early palliative care alongside cancer treatment improved quality of life and mood.
claims.supporting_passage: We randomly assigned patients with newly diagnosed metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer to receive either early palliative care integrated with standard oncologic care or standard oncologic care alone. ... Patients assigned to early palliative care had a better quality of life ... (98.0 vs. 91.5; P=0.03). In addition, fewer patients in the palliative care group than in the standard care group had depressive symptoms (16% vs. 38%, P=0.01).
claims.pico_timeframe: 151 outpatients, metastatic NSCLC; early PC + oncology vs oncology alone; 12 weeks
claims.safe_wording: In a trial of 151 people with advanced lung cancer, palliative care given alongside cancer treatment from diagnosis improved quality of life, and fewer had depressive symptoms at 12 weeks (16 in 100 vs 38 in 100).
claims.qualifications: One small US trial in lung cancer; do not generalise benefit to non-cancer illness; survival was secondary and should not lead; do not describe age as 'younger'.

numbers.meaning: depressive symptoms at 12 weeks among assessed

claims.claim: WHO definition: palliative care applicable early alongside life-prolonging therapy.
claims.safe_wording: Omit the WHO attribution; the Temel trial itself shows palliative care given alongside treatment.

claims.claim: People often associate palliative care with death and loss of hope (Zimmermann 2016).
claims.safe_wording: Omit as a finding; may say 'some people worry' as observation.
